§9.2.5 Group and Cohort Bands

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-group-and-cohort-bands · tables boundaries headers

✅ Normative

Bands over stacked grids resolve on one question: is there a shared row spine? Grids sharing one spine MUST be rendered as one table. Grids with no shared spine and no column headers MUST be rendered as one table per band, with the band as that table's header row.

Shared spine No shared spine
Row spine one continuous spine, shared label column repeated, independent per band
Column headers present, often with a numbered tier absent entirely
Rendering one table one table per cohort, band becomes its header row

The row spine is checked first, then the column headers. Those two signals decide it; the bands themselves look identical in both cases.

Group bands over a shared spine — one table

Two boxed group headers sitting over one continuous row grid that shares a left label column MUST be rendered as a single table.

|        | Loss of Income | Other         |  ← two boxed bands
| (1)    | (2)   | (3)    | (4)   | (5)   |  ← full-width numbered tier
| 2019   | 1,204 | 887    | 310   | 95    |  ← one shared row spine

The decisive signal

A full-width numbered tier is proof of single-table semantics.

If (1)…(13) runs across the whole width, the page is asserting that all those columns describe one row. Splitting there loses the row identity that spans the groups — the fact that 2019's Loss-of-Income figures and its Other figures belong to the same year.

  • The group bands MUST be rendered as spanning cells over their column ranges.
  • The numbered tier MUST be kept as a header row, not dropped as decoration. See Barely-Existing Columns and Headers§9.3.1 — dropping the numbered tier as noise also destroys the evidence that the table is one table.

Cohort bands with no column headers — one table per cohort

Same-shape grids stacked under cohort bands, with no column headers anywhere:

FEMALE
| 25 | 1.02 | 1.10 |
MALE
| 25 | 1.08 | 1.15 |

One table per cohort. The band becomes that table's header row.

Fusing these into a single table loses the row headers: with the bands demoted to ordinary rows, nothing says which block is female and which is male.

The band is a header here precisely because nothing else is — it is the only thing naming what the rows below it are.

Keeping the two apart

The two shapes look alike from a distance and resolve in opposite directions, so both checks are run deliberately:

  • Does the left label column run continuously through both bands, unrepeated? → one table.
  • Does each band restart the same labels under it, with no column headers printed anywhere? → one table per band.

Date bands and shading changes inside a single grid are a different question again — see Bands Inside the Grid§9.2.1.
